dedupe_keys.name: hospitals in hurricane katrina challenges facing custodial institutions in a disaster new orleans 2005

description: This report examines what happened in New Orleans hospitals when Hurricane Katrina's flooding cut them off in 2005, and why their experiences differed so much. After the city's infrastructure failed, about two dozen hospitals had to evacuate patients because they lost power, water and sewage service, and many needed outside help that was slow to arrive. The producers are Bradford H. Gray and Kathy Hebert of the Urban Institute, who interviewed about a dozen hospital executives, public officials and association leaders and drew on published accounts. Coverage is the New Orleans area during the week after landfall: Louisiana Hospital Association figures show 1,749 patients in the 11 hospitals surrounded by floodwater, which also sheltered more than 7,600 staff, relatives and others; at Charity Hospital, floodwater disabled generators in the basement and more than 350 patients had to be moved. The report is a free PDF (July 2006) under Urban Institute copyright. Caveats: some sources spoke only off the record during criminal investigations of patient deaths, so parts are unattributed, and the report gives no systematic data per hospital. Simulation uses: scenarios of cascading utility loss inside hospitals, placement of backup power, and the time needed to evacuate patients once a hospital loses services. Related records: the rebuilt Veterans Affairs hospital in New Orleans (case_study-new-orleans-va-hospital-flood-resilient-rebuild) shows the design response, and the Sandy case (case_study-hurricane-sandy-nyc-hospital-evacuations) a later evacuation.
